output: html_document

## 1. Load the data

Keep **penguins.csv** in the same folder as this R Markdown file. Run the chunks in order, then knit to Word. All commands use base R.

```{r load-data}
penguins <- read.csv("penguins.csv", na.strings = c("NA", ""))
colnames(penguins)
```

## 2. Check and remove missing island values

Count missing species labels. `is.na()` identifies missing values, and `sum()` counts them. A count of zero means no species labels are missing.

```{r check-missing-island}
sum(is.na(penguins$island))
```

Keep rows where island is not missing. The `!` means "not"; the comma keeps all columns. If no species labels are missing, this leaves the data unchanged. It does not change the CSV file.

```{r remove-missing-species}
penguins <- penguins[!is.na(penguins$island), ]
sum(is.na(penguins$island))
```

Only missing **species labels** are removed here. We do not remove rows because sex is missing. Use `na.rm = TRUE` to ignore missing numerical measurements in calculations.

## 3. Review plots

The red line marks the mean. These histograms combine all islands.

### Bill length

```{r review-bill_length_mm, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
hist(penguins$bill_length_mm,
     main = "Bill length: all islands",
     xlab = "Bill length (mm)",
     col = "lightblue", border = "white")
abline(v = mean(penguins$bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
       col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

### Bill depth


### Counts by species

```{r species-barplot, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
island_counts <- table(penguins$island)
island_counts

barplot(island_counts,
        main = "Number of penguins by Island",
        xlab = "Species", ylab = "Number of penguins",
        col = c("lightblue", "lightgreen", "lightpink"))
```

## 4. Calculate statistics by species

Select the same four measurement columns. Length measurements use millimeters; body mass uses grams.

```{r select-measurements}
measurements <- penguins[, c("bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm",
                             "flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g")]
```

As in the sex analysis, `aggregate()` repeats a calculation for each group. The grouping variable is now `species`. Each table has one row per species and one column per measurement.

### Mean

```{r island-mean}
aggregate(measurements,
          by = list(species = penguins$island),
          FUN = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
```

### Median

```{r island-median}
aggregate(measurements,
          by = list(species = penguins$island),
          FUN = median, na.rm = TRUE)
```

### Sample variance

```{r island-var}
aggregate(measurements,
          by = list(species = penguins$island),
          FUN = var, na.rm = TRUE)
```

### Sample standard deviation

```{r island-sd}
aggregate(measurements,
          by = list(species = penguins$island),
          FUN = sd, na.rm = TRUE)
```

`var()` and `sd()` calculate sample statistics using n - 1. SD has the original measurement's units; variance has squared units. Each column's calculation uses its available measurements.

## 5. Filter the three species

Species labels are case-sensitive: use `Adelie`, `Chinstrap`, and `Gentoo` exactly as shown. The comma selects matching rows and keeps all columns.

```{r filter-island}
biscoe_data <- penguins[penguins$island == "Biscoe", ]
dream_data <- penguins[penguins$island == "Dream", ]
torgersen_data <- penguins[penguins$island == "Torgersen", ]

nrow(biscoe_data)
nrow(dream_data)
nrow(torgersen_data)
```

## 6. Compare distributions

Make separate histograms with a red line at each group's mean. R chooses bins and axes automatically, so check the axis values when comparing plots. Bar heights are counts and depend on group size; a taller bar alone does not imply less variation.

### Bill length

```{r biscoe-bill_length_mm, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
hist(biscoe_data$bill_length_mm,
     main = "Bill length: Biscoe penguins",
     xlab = "Bill length (mm)",
     col = "lightblue", border = "white")
abline(v = mean(biscoe_data$bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
```
